title: Linked Lists
relevance: Core SDE interview and OA topic for testing in-place pointer manipulation, edge-case handling, and two-pointer techniques.

phases.goal: Establish what a linked list is, its varieties, and how it differs from arrays.

must_hit.point: A linked list is a linear structure of heap-allocated nodes, each holding data and one or more pointers to other nodes, with no O(1) random access to the i-th element.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts contiguous array indexing with pointer-chasing traversal from the head.

must_hit.point: Main varieties are singly linked (forward only), doubly linked (forward and backward), and circular (tail points back to head).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three varieties and what each pointer arrangement enables.

must_hit.point: A dummy/sentinel head that points at the real head lets insert/delete at the head use the same logic as other nodes and removes empty-list and head-change edge cases.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why a temporary node in front of head unifies pointer updates.

probes: What is a linked list, and how does access cost compare to an array?
When would you use a dummy head node?

hints.1: Think about how nodes are stored in memory versus an array.
hints.2: Cover varieties (singly/doubly/circular) and the sentinel trick for head operations.
hints.3: Nodes are heap-scattered with no O(1) indexed jump; dummy head unifies insert/delete including at head.

phases.goal: Verify correct pointer updates for build, insert, delete, reverse, and slow/fast traversal.

must_hit.point: Insert at head is O(1): new node's next points to current head, then head becomes the new node; insert at tail or position k without a tail pointer is O(N) due to traversal.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States head vs tail/position costs and the (k-1)-th predecessor walk for position insert.

must_hit.point: Delete requires bypassing the target via the predecessor's next (or prev/next on a doubly list) then freeing the node; head delete is O(1), tail or position delete is O(N).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions predecessor adjustment, free/delete, and empty/single-node edge cases.

must_hit.point: Iterative singly-list reverse uses three pointers (prev, curr, nextTemp): store next, point curr->next to prev, then advance prev and curr; recursive reverse is O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the three-pointer loop or the attach-current-to-reversed-sublist recursive step.

must_hit.point: Slow/fast (tortoise and hare): slow moves one step, fast two; when fast ends, slow is at the middle (second middle if two); same idea detects cycles when they meet.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes relative speeds and the middle or meet condition without an extra length pass.

probes: How do you insert or delete at the head versus at position k?
Walk through iterative reverse, then how slow and fast find the middle or a cycle.

hints.1: Separate the head case from cases that need a predecessor.
hints.2: For reverse, name prev/curr/nextTemp; for middle/cycle, name slow and fast step sizes.
hints.3: Head insert/delete O(1); elsewhere traverse to predecessor. Reverse flips next with three pointers. Slow+1/fast+2 yields middle or Floyd meet.

phases.goal: Contrast arrays vs lists and space/time choices among standard linked-list techniques.

must_hit.point: Lists beat arrays for O(1) insert/delete at a known position without reallocation; arrays win for O(1) indexed access and cache-friendly contiguous memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both sides: pointer local edits vs random access and locality.

must_hit.point: Cycle detection: hash set of visited nodes uses O(n) space; Floyd's slow/fast meeting uses O(1) space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares visited-set approach to tortoise-hare constant space.

must_hit.point: Merge sort suits linked lists: sequential access, O(n log n) time, with O(log n) recursion-stack space (O(1) auxiliary ignoring the stack).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why merge sort fits lists better than random-access-heavy sorts.

probes: When would you pick a linked list over an array?
How do Floyd's cycle detection and merge sort trade space versus a hash-set or array-based approach?

hints.1: Start from insert/delete versus indexing and cache behavior.
hints.2: Then compare O(n) visited-set cycle check to O(1)-space Floyd, and sorting via merge.
hints.3: Lists: O(1) known-position edit, poor locality/index. Cycles: set O(n) vs Floyd O(1). Sort lists with merge sort O(n log n).

phases.goal: Apply pointer patterns to classic interview problems: cycles, palindrome, nth-from-end, intersection, and advanced clones/flatten/k-group.

must_hit.point: After Floyd meet inside a cycle, reset slow to head and advance both one step; their next meet is the cycle start; loop length is counted by fixing slow at the meet and walking fast once around.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States reset-to-head then equal-speed meet, plus count-until-return for length.

must_hit.point: Palindrome in O(1) space: find middle, reverse second half, compare halves, optionally restore; remove nth-from-end in one pass by advancing fast n steps then moving slow/fast together, often with a dummy head.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Chains middle+reverse+compare and the n-gap two-pointer delete with dummy.

must_hit.point: Intersection in O(1) space: when A finishes list A switch to headB and when B finishes switch to headA so both walk A+B and meet at the intersection (or null).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the dual-pointer redirect so total distances match.

must_hit.point: Clone with random in O(1) extra space: interleave clones after originals, set clone random via original.random.next, then unweave; flatten merges sorted bottom-lists recursively like merge-sort merge.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Outlines weave/assign/separate for random clone and bottom-up merge for flatten.

probes: How do you find a cycle's start and its length with constant space?
How would you check palindrome, remove the nth node from the end, or clone a list with random pointers in place?

hints.1: Reuse Floyd for cycle problems; reuse middle/reverse for palindrome.
hints.2: Nth-from-end: gap of n with dummy; intersection: switch heads so paths equalize.
hints.3: Meet then reset slow to head for cycle start; count one lap for length; middle+reverse halves for palindrome; weave clones for random copy.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer a list for O(1) insertions/deletions at a known position without reallocation; prefer an array for O(1) indexed access and contiguous cache-friendly memory.
Iterative reverse uses a few pointers and O(1) space; recursive reverse is O(n) time but O(n) call-stack space.

tradeoffs.topic: Hash set vs Floyd for cycles
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A visited-node set detects cycles in O(n) time with O(n) space; Floyd's slow/fast meeting detects cycles in O(n) time with O(1) space.

tradeoffs.topic: Array copy vs in-place for palindrome / sort
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Copying values to an array is simple but O(n) space; optimal palindrome reverses the second half in place for O(1) space, and merge sort sorts a list in O(n log n) time with sequential merges instead of random-access sorts.

tradeoffs.topic: Hash map vs weave for cloning with random
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A map from original to clone uses O(n) space; weaving each clone after its original, assigning random via original.random.next, then separating restores O(1) auxiliary space.

gotchas.trap: Reassigning head while traversing and losing the rest of the list
gotchas.correction: Keep a temporary curr (or similar) for traversal; only update head when the operation intentionally changes the first node.

gotchas.trap: Dereferencing node->next or node->data without a null check
gotchas.correction: Always test for nullptr before following or reading a pointer to avoid segmentation faults.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting head/empty/single-node edge cases on insert or delete
gotchas.correction: Use a dummy head so head edits share the same predecessor logic, and explicitly handle empty list and deleting the only node.

gotchas.trap: After swapping next and prev while reversing a doubly linked list, continuing via the old next
gotchas.correction: After the swap, advance with curr = curr->prev (the original next), and return the new head from the last processed node's partner (e.g. temp->prev).

gotchas.trap: When two middle nodes exist, returning the first middle
gotchas.correction: With equal-start slow/fast stepping one and two, return the second middle when the length is even, matching the usual interview requirement.
